html:
Social across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

By nine, the social mind has shifted from the 5-7 window’s budding second-order belief tracking, display-rule mastery, and emerging reputation sensitivity into a genuinely well-informed, strategic, and norm-aware social reasoner. Nine-year-olds now succeed far more often on "advanced" mentalizing that requires embedding beliefs within beliefs and reading pragmatic intent: some 9-year-olds can distinguish sarcasm from literal criticism and from irony, recover what the speaker really meant, and even attribute why a speaker used a non-literal form (teasing, mitigation) rather than just noticing incongruity 1, 2, 3, 4. Their epistemic vigilance also sharpens: rather than trusting by default (or using basic heuristics to evaluate speakers), nine-year-olds weigh informants’ past accuracy, expertise, benevolence, and potential conflicts of interest, showing a more adult-like "knowing when to doubt" stance than seven-year-olds 5. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

In emotion understanding, nine-year-olds enter the "reflective" phase on the Test of Emotion Comprehension 6: they coordinate mixed and even conflicting emotions within a single person (e.g being happy and disappointed at the same time), differentiate inner feelings from outward displays with meta-representational justifications, and can explain how beliefs and perspectives drive affect (including in themselves) 7, 6, 8, capacities that are only nascent at seven. Knowledge about cognitive regulation also becomes explicit: they can articulate and begin to deploy cognitive reappraisal (not merely suppression) and understand that different strategies alter emotional intensity and expression, capacities that show strong gains across late childhood and are measurable in 9-12-year-olds 9, 10. Moral emotion attributions shift as well: whereas many seven-year-olds still show traces of the "happy-victimizer" pattern, nine-year-olds more reliably predict guilt or shame for wrongdoers and begin to differentiate these emotions in terms of internal standards and self-evaluation 11, 12. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Prosocial behavior shifts from predominantly sympathy-based motivation toward increasingly strategic deployment: while five-to-seven-year-olds show emerging reputation sensitivity, children aged seven to nine become proficient at instrumentally using prosocial acts to achieve self-serving goals including reputation enhancement, eliciting reciprocity, and securing future social partnerships, balancing altruistic and selfish motives with growing sophistication. This strategic capacity extends to deception, where semantic leakage control improves substantially; one study showed that, by age 8, approximately half of children can maintain consistency between initial lies and subsequent statements (feigning ignorance when asked follow-up questions), compared to the majority of younger children who immediately betray their deception 13, and children increasingly tell white lies in politeness situations despite viewing them as technically dishonest 14, demonstrating emergent capacity to navigate conflicting social rules and make strategic trade-offs between honesty norms and relationship maintenance.

Peer relationship structures become more differentiated and hierarchically organized, with stable cliques forming around shared interests and coordinated activities rather than mere proximity, sociometric hierarchies solidifying such that children show strong consensus about popular and rejected peers and actively work to improve social standing through strategic affiliation and self-presentation, and friendship conceptions shifting from "fair-weather cooperation" (expecting immediate reciprocity) toward more psychologically grounded bonds emphasizing loyalty, trust, and genuine care for the other’s welfare independent of transactional exchange 15. Children also develop more nuanced understanding of social influence and peer dynamics, becoming increasingly aware that they are being evaluated by others and that different peers hold different social perspectives (extending the simpler "audience effects" of younger ages) 16, enabling more sophisticated navigation of the reputational landscape while simultaneously making them vulnerable to heightened social anxiety as they track their standing within increasingly complex peer networks.

Across major theoretical frameworks, nine-year-olds sit at the cusp of "big-kid" social cognition. In Piagetian terms they are firmly in the concrete-operational period and, in Piaget’s moral theory, begin the shift toward autonomous morality ( 9-10 y): they begin to decenter from outcomes to intentions (moral judgements are outcome-based until  8 17) and treat rules as human agreements rather than absolutes 18, 19. In Selman’s role-taking model they are characteristically at Level 2 (reciprocal, self-reflective;  8-10 y), able to reason about how the other sees them and how they appear to the other, though not yet to coordinate multiple perspectives from a generalized third party 20. Social-domain theory finds that by this age children reliably treat moral norms as authority-independent and generalizable while viewing conventional rules as context-bound 21; meanwhile, Kohlberg’s accounts place many at the boundary between preconventional self-interest and emerging conventional concern for interpersonal expectations and norm maintenance 22. From sociocultural and information-processing views, the internalization of private speech into inner speech together with middle-childhood gains in executive control makes social reasoning more planful and strategic, improving encoding/interpretation of social cues, generation of response options, and evaluation of consequences with affect integrated 23, 24.
